PODCAST SPONSORSHIP RATE CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What should you charge for a podcast ad?

Enter your average downloads per episode, niche, and read type below. This turns those numbers into a price range for each common ad placement — a pre-roll, a mid-roll, and a post-roll spot — using the same cost-per-1000-downloads logic podcast ad marketplaces and network rate cards use, applied to your own show instead of a marketplace's cut-taking listing.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

Also selling ads on a newsletter alongside the show? See the newsletter sponsorship rate calculator. Also monetizing a social following? See the brand deal rate calculator for pricing that channel too. Also streaming on Twitch? See the Twitch payout calculator for real take-home from subs and Bits.

Your show's numbers

Enter your numbers above and click Calculate my rates.

Suggested price range by placement

PlacementSuggested range (per spot)

What this does and doesn't do

This applies commonly cited podcast-ad-market CPM-per-1000-downloads benchmark ranges — wide ranges, by design — to the downloads, niche, and read type you enter. It does not know your specific niche's current market, your show's engagement or conversion history, or what a specific sponsor is willing to pay this quarter. Treat the output as a starting point for a negotiation, not a quote.

Already listed on Podcorn's marketplace, or thinking about it? See how this free calculator differs from a marketplace listing and its commission. Pricing off one flat "average podcast CPM" number instead? See why a flat rate misprices individual spots.

Common questions

How much should I charge for a podcast ad?

It depends on your average downloads per episode, niche, which ad placement you're selling, and whether it's host-read or produced. This calculator applies commonly cited market CPM-per-1000-downloads ranges to your own numbers to give a starting price range for a pre-roll, mid-roll, or post-roll spot.

Why does this calculate price from downloads instead of subscriber or listener count?

Sponsors are paying for a spot that actually got served. Podcast ad marketplaces and network rate cards routinely price against downloads in the first 7 days of an episode (the industry-standard IAB/Podtrac window), not a lifetime subscriber count that includes people who stopped listening long ago. See why that gap can mean a 4x overask if you price off the wrong number.

Is this price a guarantee of what a sponsor will pay?

No. It is a starting point for negotiation based on general market ranges, not a quote, valuation, or offer performed on your behalf. Actual rates vary by audience quality, host endorsement strength, niche demand, and how much a specific sponsor wants your specific audience this quarter.

What is the difference between a host-read and a produced ad?

A host-read ad is read live by the host in their own voice and words, usually woven into the episode — it commands a premium because listeners trust the host's personal endorsement. A produced ad is a pre-recorded, studio-produced spot dropped into the episode, similar to traditional radio or streaming audio ads, and typically prices lower.

vs-a-flat-industry-average-cpm.html.text:
← Podcast Sponsorship Rate Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat industry-average CPM

A rate report's single "average podcast CPM" number prices a pre-roll, a mid-roll, and a post-roll spot identically. This calculator's benchmark ranges price them differently — and for a real show, using the flat number on all three can mean underselling your best slot and overpricing your weakest one in the same pitch.

What each one prices

A flat industry-average CPM is the single cost-per-1,000- downloads figure podcast ad rate reports and blog posts commonly cite as "the average podcast CPM." Multiply it by your downloads in thousands and you have a price — the same price for a pre-roll spot, a mid-roll spot, and a post-roll spot, and the same price whether the ad is host-read or produced, because a single average has no input for placement or read type at all.

This calculator applies a separate benchmark CPM range to each placement, because sponsors do not value them equally: mid-roll ads sit inside the episode where listener drop-off is lowest and are commonly cited as commanding the highest rate, pre-roll comes next, and post-roll — played after much of the audience has already stopped listening — is priced lowest of the three. It also discounts a produced spot from the host-read benchmark, since a pre-recorded ad carries no live host endorsement.

Placement (8,000 downloads/ep, business, host-read)Flat $25 average CPMThis calculator's range
Pre-roll$200$160 – $224
Mid-roll$200$240 – $360
Post-roll$200$120 – $160

$25 per 1,000 downloads sits inside commonly cited ranges for a business show and is used here only to illustrate the shape of the gap, not as a claim about any specific report's published figure. Applied flat across all three spots it prints the same $200 for each — on the mid-roll, that undersells this calculator's own low end by $40 and its high end by $160; on the post-roll, it asks a sponsor to pay $40–$80 above this calculator's range for the least-watched slot of the three. Both mistakes come from the same flat number, in the same negotiation.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Why does a flat average undersell mid-roll?It blends a high-value slot in with a lower-value one and lands in between. This calculator's rate range prices mid-roll on its own benchmark.
Why does a flat average overprice post-roll?Same blending, other direction: it pulls the lowest-value slot up toward the average of all three.
Does a flat CPM adjust for host-read vs. produced?No — one number for both. This calculator discounts produced spots from the host-read benchmark.
Is my downloads, niche, and read-type data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything runs in your browser; nothing is sent to any server.

A flat average is a reasonable one-number anchor before you have a show's actual numbers in front of you. It is not built to price three spots that are not worth the same amount — which is what pricing by placement and read type does, for free, from numbers your own hosting dashboard already reports.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

What is a flat industry-average CPM?

A single cost-per-1,000-downloads figure — podcast ad rate reports and blog posts commonly cite one number as "the average podcast CPM" — multiplied against a show's downloads to get an ad price. It needs one number and gives the same answer for a pre-roll, mid-roll, or post-roll spot, and the same answer whether the ad is host-read or produced, because it has no input for either.

Why does a flat CPM misprice individual spots so often?

Because a single average blends three placements that sponsors do not value equally. Mid-roll ads sit inside the episode where listener drop-off is lowest and typically command the highest CPM; pre-roll and especially post-roll are worth less. A flat average sits between all three, so it understates the mid-roll and overstates the post-roll for the same show at the same time.

Does the gap matter at typical show sizes, or only at scale?

It shows up at ordinary sizes. An 8,000-download business show pricing three spots off one flat average leaves real money on the mid-roll and asks a sponsor to overpay for the post-roll — both in the same negotiation, from the same flat number.

Does a flat CPM adjust for host-read vs. produced the way this calculator does?

No — a flat average has no read-type input, so it prices a live host endorsement the same as a pre-recorded studio spot. This calculator's ranges discount produced spots from the host-read benchmark, since a produced ad carries no live endorsement.

Open the Podcast Sponsorship Rate Calculator to run your own numbers, or see how this differs from listing on Podcorn.

No warranty. This free tool is not financial, legal, tax, or business advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or your own judgment about a specific deal. It cannot promise any sponsor will pay a given price and does not perform, guarantee, or represent any negotiation on your behalf. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device. This page describes a generic flat-CPM pricing habit passed around across podcast ad rate reports and blog posts; it names no specific company, product, or publication, and it is not a claim that any one source states the figure exactly this way.

Free and open source. If it helps you set an ask, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-podcorn.html.text:
← Podcast sponsorship rate calculator

This calculator vs. Podcorn

Podcorn is a self-serve podcast sponsorship marketplace: you create a show profile, brands browse and send offers (or you pitch them directly), and Podcorn handles matching, contracting, and payment for a commission on the value of each deal it processes.

That makes Podcorn the right choice for finding brands you don't already have, and running the whole matching, contracting, and payment process through a marketplace. This page answers a narrower question: for a sponsor you already have -- your own network, a cold pitch, a returning advertiser -- what should you actually charge, free, with no profile and no cut of what you negotiate directly.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I don't have a sponsor yet -- where do I find one? Podcorn's marketplace, or another advertiser network.
I already have a sponsor (or a lead) -- what should I quote them? This calculator -- enter your numbers, get a price range immediately, nothing listed.
What's a typical range across the whole market, by show size? Podcorn's own market data, drawn from deals on its marketplace.
What's a defensible range for my specific downloads, niche, and read type? This calculator's own CPM-per-downloads math.
Can I get an answer without creating a profile or giving up a commission? This calculator -- a static page, no sign-up, no booking, no cut.
Get a price range now

This tool needs no account and lists nothing: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your downloads, niche, read type, and every other figure stay on this device -- nothing is uploaded anywhere, there is no marketplace listing, and no commission on whatever you and your sponsor agree to.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Podcorn?

They solve different problems. Podcorn is a marketplace: you create a show profile, brands browse and send sponsorship offers (or you pitch them), and Podcorn handles matching, contracting, and payment in exchange for a commission on the deal. This page is a free calculator: no profile, no brand discovery, no commission. You enter your average downloads per episode, niche, and read type, and it gives you a price range to quote a sponsor you already found yourself -- through your own network, a cold pitch, or a returning advertiser.

Does Podcorn price the same way this calculator does?

Not exactly the same inputs. On Podcorn, podcasters typically set their own asking price per deliverable and brands accept, counter, or pass, with the platform's own market data informing what a competitive ask looks like. This calculator has no marketplace data to draw on; it applies commonly cited CPM-per-1000-downloads benchmark ranges to your own downloads, niche, and read type instead, so the range is grounded in published market rates for your show's numbers rather than what Podcorn's brand pool happened to offer this quarter.

Is Podcorn free?

Not to transact through. Podcorn does not charge podcasters to create a profile, but marketplaces like it commonly take a percentage-based commission on the value of a booked deal -- check Podcorn's current published terms for the exact rate, since fee structures change. This calculator has no listing, no deal flow, and takes no cut of anything -- it is a free static page that only computes a price range.

Is this page affiliated with Podcorn?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Podcorn, and this page is not a review of it. Podcorn is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is for. Marketplace mechanics described above are drawn from Podcorn's own public description of its service rather than measured by us, and marketplace fees, plans and requirements change -- check Podcorn's current terms on their site before relying on any detail here.

why-downloads-not-subscribers.html.text:
← Podcast Sponsorship Rate Calculator

Why podcast ad pricing uses downloads, not subscribers

A podcast with 40,000 people subscribed in a podcast app is not a 40,000-download show, and a sponsor's ad-ops team knows the difference even if the pitch doesn't say so. This calculator prices off downloads in an episode's first 7 days for the same reason every marketplace and rate card does: it's the number that measures who actually received the ad, not who once tapped follow.

Open this example on the calculator

Two different numbers, and only one of them is what a sponsor is buying

A subscriber or follower count is a standing total that only grows: everyone who ever subscribed stays counted, including people who stopped listening months ago, downgraded their queue, or never opened the app again. A 7-day download count is a fresh measurement, taken every episode, of how many people actually requested that specific episode's audio file in a defined window after it went live. One rises forever; the other tells you what happened this week.

Sponsors pay for the second number, because it's the one that describes who was actually served the ad. Podcast ad marketplaces and network rate cards are built on it, and so is the industry's own measurement standard: the IAB Podcast Measurement Technical Guidelines, which define the download window as the 7 days following an episode's release -- widely referred to as the IAB/Podtrac methodology. A number quoted any other way (since release with no cutoff, over 30 or 90 days, or a subscriber count standing in for either) is measuring something else, and a buyer whose own systems report 7-day downloads has no way to compare it.

Worked example: 40,000 subscribers, 10,000 real downloads

Take a business-niche show with a host-read mid-roll slot, 40,000 total subscribers across podcast apps, and 10,000 downloads in a typical episode's first 7 days -- a plausible gap, since plenty of subscribers stop listening without unsubscribing. Pricing the same mid-roll spot off each number gives two very different asks:

Priced offCount usedMid-roll range
7-day downloads (correct)10,000$300–$450
Total app subscribers (wrong)40,000$1,200–$1,800

That's a 4x overask for identical inventory -- not because the download-based number is conservative, but because the subscriber count was never a measure of who receives a given episode's ad in the first place. A sponsor's ad-ops team, pricing by their own downloads-based benchmarks, won't negotiate that gap down; they'll read the pitch as unmeasured and move to a show whose numbers already match how the industry buys.

Common questions

Why does podcast ad pricing use downloads, not subscriber count?

Because a sponsor is paying for a spot that actually got served, not a standing audience that may or may not still be listening. Podcast ad marketplaces and network rate cards price against downloads within the first 7 days of an episode going live -- the industry-standard IAB/Podtrac measurement window -- rather than a subscriber or follower count, which includes anyone who subscribed once and stopped listening, and never shrinks even as a show's real audience does.

What exactly counts as a download in the 7-day window?

A request for the episode's audio file, deduplicated by your hosting platform's analytics, counted from the moment the episode goes live through the following 7 days. That window is the IAB Podcast Measurement Technical Guidelines' own definition, which is why sponsors' ad-ops teams already expect a number measured this way -- a total quoted over 30 or 90 days, or since the episode's release with no cutoff, is a different, larger, and non-comparable figure.

How much would pricing off subscribers instead of downloads actually change my ask?

On this calculator's own numbers: a business-niche, host-read show with 40,000 total app subscribers but 10,000 real downloads in an episode's first 7 days should price a mid-roll at $300-$450. Quoting off the subscriber count instead -- treating 40,000 as the reach -- prices the same spot at $1,200-$1,800, a 4x overask. A sponsor's ad-ops team, who already measures by 7-day downloads, will not read that as an aggressive opener; they will read it as a number that does not match their own data and move to the next show.

Where do I find my show's actual 7-day downloads?

Your hosting platform's own analytics dashboard -- Spotify for Podcasters, Apple Podcasts Connect, Libsyn, Buzzsprout, and most other hosts all report downloads by episode with a rolling window you can set to 7 days. That is the number to enter here, not a lifetime download total, not an RSS subscriber count, and not app-reported "followers", each of which measures something a sponsor is not paying for.
